text: Can someone explain whats the 1%low and 0.1% low ?
author: @yassine9490

text: The lowest 1% and 0.1% fps results recorded during the benchmark.
author: @optimumtech

text:
1% or .1% low are worst case scenario framerates. 
For example, by every 100 seconds of benchmarking, the 1 second out of those 100 in which the framerate is at its lowest is the 1% low.
In another example, for every 1000 seconds of benchmarking, the 1 second out of 1000 in which the framerate is at its lowest is the .1% low.

Another metric that's important is frametimes. First you divide 1 second into 60 (for 60 FPS). In such case, every frame must be buffered at a rate of ~16.7ms per frame for a perfect 60FPS framerate and frametime (16.7ms * 60 = 1000ms). If a frame stays longer on the screen, framespikes appear and as a result you'll see some stuttering. When a frame stays on the screen longer than 16.7ms, you'll have less frames per second. This is linked to 1% and .1% lows, since you might have this event occurring at times (the rarer it happens, the better for gameplay stability).

1% and .1% lows are important, because the closer those framerates are to the average, the tighter the frametimes and thus, the more stable and less stuttery/jittery the gameplay is. It's not all about the average framerate.

text: The answer has always been clear: don't start thinking about buying a graphics card when the newest and hottest card is around the corner! Even if the card you want is about to get cheaper! It's not worth it! Why? Because the rest of the industry has already moved on to the next gen requirements well before the next gen cards reach the market! For example, if you're only starting to think about buying a new card now and don't have the money, start raising money now! This way, by the time the next-next gen top card reaches the market, you can buy it. There's no point in buying the cheaper card just to use it at medium, and pretty soon at low settings with most of the upcoming games and then just having to ditch it or look for another card yet again in just 2 year's time. The industry has fooled people into buying less performant hardware than they could have for a very long time by abusing market segmentation. I'm not talking about the really poor people that can't afford more than an entry-level card. I'm talking about the people that can afford at least a mid-level card. Unless those people sold a kidney and they only got the price of a mid-level card, which case they should probably buy the card they can afford and not think about selling another body part. But otherwise, stop aiming for mid-level cards. Aim for the top level card of the current generation. And maybe wait a bit before buying it, just in case nVidia decides to put a fscking Ti sticker on the top card and sell that one as the "fortuitous" king of the hill just 2 months after releasing the supposedly best card of their gaming lineup and ask the same price just to spite you. I think this is the advice people should be getting.

text: this is a misconception. miners look for efficiency over brute force, meaning almost all, if not all, mining cards have had their power limit bumped down to a point where it still performs reasonably well, but consumes considerably less power. that's usually about 70%, depending on card model, meaning they've been working at 70% of their capacity, barely heating up or breaking a sweat, unlike us gamers, where we immediately (at least I do) bump the power limit to as far as it will go for better performance during the couple of hours it's actually in use. plus, video cards are not cars with moving parts that wear out with use. MTBF for most electronic components go well over several tens of thousands of hours of use. a used mining card has pretty much the same failure chance than a used gaming card in the end.... and if you get a card from one of those manufacturers with transferable warranty, like evga, you're still fully covered in case something happens. they are insane deals right now. got an evga GTX 1080 Ti SC2 for less than $500 a couple of weeks ago.
author: @emp1985

text: EVGA is some countries don't offer transferable warranty anymore since May 2018. Buying secondhand goods always carry risks but it's arguably more risky to buy from a miner than a gamer since gamers don't run their cards 24/7. Total runtime for a last gen card from gamer is probably around 6 months at most while for a miner could be up to 2 years straight (even with efficiency tuning and care taken).
